triage.name: Corneal abrasion
triage.reason: Acute painful red eye after trauma or foreign body; classic history and exam with fluorescein staining make a good case with look-alikes like corneal ulcer and uveitis.

demographics: Common in people who work with their hands or play contact sports
More common in contact lens wearers

risk_factors.text: Recent eye trauma or foreign body
Occupational exposure to dust, metal or wood particles

social_history: Works in construction, farming or other dusty trades
exposures: Airborne dust, grit or metal shavings
Fingernail or foreign object to the eye

chief_complaints.text: It feels like something is stuck in my eye
My eye is red and watery

hpi.onset: Sudden, right after the injury or foreign body exposure
hpi.progression: Pain and tearing start immediately and stay constant; they do not worsen over days unless infection develops
hpi.location: One eye, over the surface of the eye
hpi.radiation: Pain can radiate to the brow or temple
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; often 6–8/10 and worse with blinking
hpi.timing: Constant, worse with blinking and bright light
relieving: Topical anesthetic in the emergency department
pertinent_negatives: Severe deep eye pain with vision loss

argues_against: Marked vision loss suggests corneal ulcer or uveitis
Flashes and floaters suggest retinal detachment
Focal neurologic deficit suggests a different cause
Fever suggests infection rather than simple abrasion

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not report a clear injury; they present with crying, eye rubbing, refusal to open the eye and light sensitivity.
missing_classic_features: Clear history of trauma or foreign body

atypical.how_it_differs: May have reduced corneal sensation and report less pain despite a significant abrasion; dry eye and prior eye disease are more common.
Healing is slower and there is a higher risk of progression to infectious keratitis, so a red painful eye after minor trauma needs closer follow-up.

general.mild: Alert, uncomfortable, holds the affected eye closed or shields it from light
general.moderate: Ill at ease, keeps the eye closed, avoids bright light, tears running down the cheek
general.severe: Distressed, blepharospasm, reluctant to open the eye, marked photophobia
general.critical: Not typical for an uncomplicated abrasion; consider a retained foreign body, corneal ulcer or globe injury

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye separately with a Snellen chart before any eye manipulation
findings.finding: Mildly reduced visual acuity in the affected eye that improves with pinhole or after blinking

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in daylight
findings.finding: Diffuse conjunctival redness of the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Instill fluorescein and examine the cornea under cobalt blue light with a slit lamp or Wood lamp
findings.finding: A focal area of fluorescein uptake on the corneal surface outlining the epithelial defect

findings.maneuver: Examine the corneal surface with a slit lamp after fluorescein
findings.finding: A visible epithelial defect or irregularity of the corneal surface

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to describe the sensation in the eye
findings.finding: Reports of a gritty or foreign body sensation in the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Shine a light into the eye or ask the patient to look at a bright light
findings.finding: Pain or aversion to light in the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eye and lower lid for excess tears
findings.finding: Excess tearing from the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's ability to keep the eye open
findings.finding: Involuntary eyelid spasm or squinting of the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Swing a light between the eyes and observe the direct and consensual pupillary responses
findings.finding: No relative afferent pupillary defect; both pupils constrict normally

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow a finger through the cardinal directions of gaze
findings.finding: Full, painless extraocular movements without diplopia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctival sac and lid margins for discharge
Inspect the limbus and perilimbal vessels under magnification
findings.finding: No perilimbal or ciliary injection; redness is diffuse and peripheral

findings.maneuver: Examine the cornea under slit lamp for opacities or infiltrates
findings.finding: No corneal opacity, infiltrate or white spot

findings.maneuver: Inspect the anterior chamber for a fluid level
findings.finding: No layering of pus or cells in the anterior chamber

findings.maneuver: Evert the upper eyelid and sweep the fornices with a cotton swab
findings.finding: No retained foreign body on the conjunctiva, tarsal plate or cornea

findings.maneuver: Test facial sensation to light touch in the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve

imaging.study: Slit lamp examination with fluorescein staining
imaging.preferred_when: All patients with a red, painful eye after trauma or foreign body exposure

findings.text: Focal area of fluorescein uptake outlining the corneal epithelial defect
Visible epithelial defect or surface irregularity of the cornea
No corneal infiltrate, opacity or white spot
No retained foreign body on the cornea, conjunctiva or tarsal plate
No cells or fluid level in the anterior chamber

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected retained intraocular or intraorbital foreign body, or concern for globe rupture

findings.text: No intraocular or intraorbital foreign body
No globe rupture or intraocular air
Metallic or radiopaque foreign body if one is retained

initial.test: Slit lamp examination with fluorescein staining
initial.why: Confirms the corneal epithelial defect and looks for a retained foreign body, infiltrate or anterior chamber cells

supporting.why: Localizes a suspected retained foreign body or evaluates for globe rupture
supporting.only_if: a retained intraocular or intraorbital foreign body is suspected, or globe rupture is a concern

not_indicated.why: No role in an uncomplicated corneal abrasion
No role in an uncomplicated corneal abrasion
No role in an uncomplicated corneal abrasion
No role in an uncomplicated corneal abrasion

decision_points: Check visual acuity and perform fluorescein staining before any eye manipulation
Evert the upper eyelid to look for a retained foreign body
Consider orbital CT when a retained intraocular or intraorbital foreign body or globe rupture is suspected
Contact lens wearers need closer follow-up and coverage for Pseudomonas

differential.name: Corneal ulcer (infectious keratitis)
differential.why_considered: Red, painful, watery eye with photophobia and a foreign body sensation, especially in contact lens wearers
differential.trigger: Contact lens wear, purulent discharge, or a white spot on the cornea

history: Contact lens wear, especially overnight or extended wear
Pain and photophobia worsening over days rather than starting abruptly after trauma
exam: Corneal opacity, infiltrate or white spot on slit lamp
Marked visual loss that does not improve with pinhole
labs: Corneal scraping for Gram stain and culture if a corneal ulcer is suspected
imaging: Slit lamp shows an infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect rather than a clean epithelial defect alone

differential.name: Anterior uveitis (iritis)
differential.why_considered: Painful red eye with photophobia and tearing
differential.trigger: Deep aching eye pain with ciliary flush and no clear history of trauma

history: Deep, aching eye pain rather than a gritty surface sensation
No clear history of trauma or foreign body
Associated autoimmune disease or prior episodes
exam: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber
Constricted pupil and photophobia out of proportion to surface findings
labs: Consider HLA-B27, ANA or infectious serologies if recurrent or bilateral
imaging: Slit lamp shows anterior chamber cells and flare without a corneal epithelial defect

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Severe eye pain with redness, tearing and blurred vision
differential.trigger: Severe pain with headache, nausea or vomiting and a mid-dilated fixed pupil

history: Severe pain with headache, nausea and vomiting
Older age, hyperopia or known narrow angles
imaging: Tonometry shows markedly elevated intraocular pressure; gonioscopy shows closed angles

differential.name: Retained corneal or conjunctival foreign body
differential.why_considered: Persistent foreign body sensation and tearing after exposure to dust or metal
differential.trigger: Foreign body sensation that persists after fluorescein staining shows only a small defect

history: Exposure to metal grinding, wood or dust
Symptoms persist or worsen after initial treatment
exam: Visible foreign body on the cornea, conjunctiva or under the upper eyelid
Linear vertical corneal scratches suggesting a foreign body under the upper lid
imaging: Slit lamp with eyelid eversion shows the retained foreign body
Orbital CT if an intraocular or intraorbital foreign body is suspected

differential.name: Bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, irritated eye with tearing and discharge

history: Mucopurulent discharge with matted lashes on waking
No history of trauma or foreign body
Often bilateral or spreading from one eye to the other
exam: Diffuse conjunctival injection without corneal epithelial defect
No fluorescein uptake on the cornea

differential.name: Viral conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, watery eye with foreign body sensation and photophobia

history: Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts
exam: Diffuse conjunctival injection, often with follicles
No corneal epithelial defect on fluorescein staining

differential.name: Globe rupture
differential.why_considered: Severe eye pain and redness after trauma
differential.trigger: High-velocity trauma, marked vision loss, or an irregular pupil

history: High-velocity trauma such as hammering metal or a projectile
Marked vision loss immediately after injury
imaging: Orbital CT without contrast shows globe deformity, intraocular air or a retained intraocular foreign body

severity.mild: Small, superficial epithelial defect with mild pain, tearing and photophobia; visual acuity normal or near normal; no infiltrate or anterior chamber cells
severity.moderate: Larger or central defect with moderate to severe pain, blepharospasm and photophobia; mildly reduced visual acuity that improves with pinhole; no infection
severity.severe: Extensive or recurrent defect, or an abrasion in a contact lens wearer with increasing pain, discharge or a corneal infiltrate suggesting early infection
severity.critical: Not typical for an uncomplicated corneal abrasion; consider globe rupture, retained intraocular foreign body or a rapidly progressive corneal ulcer with hypopyon

red_flags.meaning: Suggests corneal ulcer, uveitis, hyphema or globe injury rather than a simple abrasion

red_flags.finding: Purulent discharge or a white spot on the cornea
red_flags.meaning: Suggests infectious keratitis, which needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation and topical antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Contact lens wear with increasing pain after 24 hours
red_flags.meaning: Higher risk of Pseudomonas keratitis; needs close follow-up and antipseudomonal coverage

red_flags.finding: High-velocity trauma, irregular pupil or shallow anterior chamber
red_flags.meaning: Possible globe rupture; do not manipulate the eye and obtain urgent ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, nausea or vomiting with a mid-dilated fixed pupil
red_flags.meaning: Suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma with elevated intraocular pressure

red_flags.finding: Flashes, floaters or a curtain over the vision
red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal detachment or posterior segment injury

complications.name: Recurrent corneal erosion
clues: Recurrent morning eye pain and tearing weeks after the initial injury
History of a prior abrasion, especially from a fingernail or paper

complications.name: Secondary bacterial keratitis
clues: Increasing pain, discharge or photophobia after 24–48 hours
Corneal infiltrate or white spot on slit lamp

complications.name: Corneal scarring
clues: Central abrasion with persistent blurred vision

complications.name: Traumatic iritis
clues: Deep aching pain and marked photophobia
Anterior chamber cells and flare on slit lamp

special_populations.differences: Young children may not report a clear injury and present with crying, eye rubbing, refusal to open the eye and light sensitivity; examination may require gentle restraint or sedation.
Reduced corneal sensation can make pain milder than expected; dry eye and prior eye disease are more common, and healing may be slower.
Slower healing and higher risk of progression to infectious keratitis; arrange close follow-up and consider early ophthalmology referral.
Impaired epithelial healing may prolong recovery; monitor closely for secondary infection.

key_questions.question: Did something get into your eye or hit your eye, and when did it happen?
key_questions.looking_for: A clear injury or foreign body exposure immediately before the pain started

key_questions.question: What were you doing when it started — grinding metal, woodworking, yard work, or playing sports?
key_questions.looking_for: High-risk activity that suggests a retained foreign body or high-velocity injury

key_questions.question: Does it feel like something is stuck in your eye, and does blinking make it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gritty foreign body sensation and pain worse with blinking

key_questions.question: Is your vision blurred or lost in that eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild blurring that clears with blinking or pinhole; marked or persistent loss suggests a deeper injury

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses? Did you sleep in them or wear them past their schedule?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear, especially overnight or extended wear, raises concern for Pseudomonas keratitis

key_questions.question: Is there any discharge or pus from the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in a simple abrasion; purulent discharge suggests infectious keratitis

key_questions.question: Are you sensitive to light, and does the pain feel like it is deep inside the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Surface photophobia from the abrasion; deep aching pain with marked photophobia suggests iritis

key_questions.question: Have you had eye surgery, a prior abrasion, or a recurrent erosion?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior abrasion or erosion increases the risk of recurrence; recent surgery changes the workup

key_questions.question: Do you have any autoimmune disease or prior episodes of a red, painful eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent or bilateral episodes suggest uveitis rather than trauma

key_questions.question: Do you have flashes, floaters, or a curtain over your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests retinal detachment or posterior segment injury

key_questions.question: Do you have a headache, nausea, or vomiting along with the eye pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present with a mid-dilated fixed pupil suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood thinners or do you have a bleeding disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulation or coagulopathy raises concern for hyphema or more serious trauma

reasoning_points: Sudden onset of a painful, red, watery eye immediately after trauma or foreign body exposure
Gritty foreign body sensation with pain worse on blinking and bright light
Visual acuity normal or only mildly reduced and improving with pinhole
Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light shows a focal corneal epithelial defect
No corneal infiltrate, opacity, hypopyon or purulent discharge to suggest infection
Upper eyelid everted and fornices swept to exclude a retained foreign body
Contact lens wear and high-velocity trauma considered because they change management and follow-up
Look-alikes such as corneal ulcer, anterior uveitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma and globe rupture excluded

easy: Clear history of a fingernail, branch or foreign body to the eye
Classic gritty pain, tearing and photophobia in one eye
Fluorescein staining shows a focal epithelial defect
No infiltrate, discharge or vision loss
medium: Contact lens wearer with a red painful eye where keratitis must be excluded
Small abrasion with minimal findings on external inspection
Symptoms out of proportion to a subtle epithelial defect
Young child who will not open the eye or give a clear history
hard: Metallic foreign body exposure with a retained intraocular foreign body or globe rupture concern
Older adult with reduced corneal sensation and milder pain than expected
Immunocompromised or diabetic patient with slow healing and risk of secondary infection
Recurrent morning pain and tearing suggesting recurrent corneal erosion rather than a new abrasion
